A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: What are the two types of fluid flow?
A.explain: The two types of fluid flow taught here are streamline (also called laminar) and turbulent. Laminar flow is smooth and orderly in parallel layers; turbulent flow is disordered and swirling. Rotational/irrotational, steady/unsteady, and compressible/incompressible are other fluid classifications, not the pair asked for.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Which statement best describes laminar blood flow?
options: Flow that always produces an audible murmur
Irregular swirling, with layers mixing freely
Smooth, orderly flow in parallel layers
Flow that occurs in veins and nowhere else
A.explain: Laminar flow is smooth and orderly, with blood moving in parallel layers. Swirls and murmurs belong to turbulence, and laminar flow is not limited to veins.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Which statement best describes turbulent blood flow?
options: Smooth, orderly flow in parallel layers
Irregular swirling once speed is very high
Flow that is confined to the aorta
Flow with no energy loss or added resistance
A.explain: Turbulent flow is irregular swirling, and it appears when speed becomes very high. Parallel layers are laminar, the aorta is not the only site, and turbulence dissipates energy and raises resistance.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Normal blood flow in a healthy artery is:
options: A mix of laminar and turbulent
A.explain: Normal blood flow in a healthy artery is laminar: smooth and orderly. Turbulence appears when the vessel is narrowed or when velocity becomes very high. A healthy artery with normal flow maintains laminar conditions.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Blood flow through a narrowed artery is expected to be:
options: Identical to flow in a wide artery
A.explain: A narrowed artery raises speed by continuity and can push the flow into turbulence. It is not forced to stay laminar or stationary, and the narrower geometry does change the flow.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Mass flow rate is defined as: (Note: mass flow rate ṁ may also be written as Q: Q = ρAv.)
options: Mass of fluid passing a point per unit time
Volume of fluid passing a point per unit time
Force of fluid on a wall per unit time
Pressure of fluid at a point per unit time
A.explain: Mass flow rate is the mass of fluid that passes a fixed point in unit time. Volume flow rate is the volume version of the same idea. Force and pressure are not flow rates.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Which of the following is the correct final formula for mass flow rate? (Note: mass flow rate ṁ may also be written as Q: Q = ρAv.)
A.explain: Mass flow rate equals density times area times speed. The other three expressions invert or rearrange the product and do not give mass per time.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Volume flow rate is calculated as:
A.explain: Volume flow rate is the product of cross-sectional area and speed. Density times that product is mass flow rate. The inverted forms do not give volume per time.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: The equation of continuity in its general form is:
options: ρ₁ A₁ v₁ = ρ₂ A₂ v₂
ρ₁ A₁ / v₁ = ρ₂ A₂ / v₂
A.explain: The general continuity equation equates mass flow rate at two points: density times area times speed is constant. The pure area-speed form holds only when density is the same at both points.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: For an incompressible fluid, the equation of continuity simplifies to:
options: ρ₁ A₁ v₁ = ρ₂ A₂ v₂
A.explain: When density is constant, it cancels and continuity reduces to area times speed. The general form still contains density, and the inverted ratios do not conserve volume flow.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: A blood vessel narrows from A₁ = 2.0×10⁻⁴ m² (v₁ = 0.40 m/s) to A₂ = 1.0×10⁻⁴ m². What is the new speed if the blood is incompressible?
A.explain: Area times speed is constant, so 2.0×10⁻⁴ × 0.40 = 1.0×10⁻⁴ × v₂. That gives v₂ = 0.80 m/s. Halving the area doubles the speed.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: In laminar flow, where is the velocity of the blood highest?
options: In the centre of the vessel
A.explain: In laminar flow the speed is highest in the centre and falls to zero at the wall. It is not uniform, and the pattern is not limited to veins.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: What is the velocity profile of laminar blood flow described as?
A.explain: Laminar flow has a parabolic profile: fastest in the centre, zero at the wall. A flat profile, random swirls, or a wall maximum describe other regimes.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: In turbulent blood flow, how do the layers move?
A.explain: Turbulent layers mix and form eddies. Smooth parallel layers are laminar, wall-only motion and zero relative speed are not turbulence.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Which of the following is not a cause of turbulent blood flow?
options: Very low speed in a wide uniform vessel
A.explain: High speed, narrowing, and irregular walls favour turbulence. Very low speed in a wide uniform vessel keeps the flow laminar.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Which of the following is a consequence of turbulent blood flow?
options: Silent flow with no energy loss
Audible murmurs and extra energy loss
A.explain: Turbulence produces murmurs and dissipates extra energy. It raises resistance rather than lowering it, and the profile is not flat or silent.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: What is the difference between mass flow rate and volume flow rate?
options: Mass flow rate includes density; volume flow rate does not
Volume flow rate includes density; mass flow rate does not
Mass flow rate is measured in m³/s
A.explain: Mass flow rate is ρAv; volume flow rate is Av. Density appears only in the mass version. They are not the same, and mass flow is in kg/s.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Blood flows through a vessel of cross-sectional area 3.0×10⁻⁴ m² at 0.30 m/s. The vessel narrows to 1.0×10⁻⁴ m². What is the new speed, if the fluid is incompressible?
A.explain: Continuity for an incompressible fluid gives A1 v1 = A2 v2, so v2 = 3.0×10⁻⁴ × 0.30 / 1.0×10⁻⁴ = 0.90 m/s. 0.10 m/s inverts the area ratio, 0.30 m/s assumes speed is unchanged, and 2.7 m/s uses a ratio of 9.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Which pair of conditions can raise blood speed or otherwise favour turbulent flow?
options: A narrowed vessel, and a damaged or irregular valve
No blood movement, and a perfectly uniform vessel
A narrowed vessel, and a perfectly uniform vessel of unchanged area
A damaged valve, and a complete absence of blood movement
A.explain: A narrowed vessel raises speed by continuity, and a damaged or irregular valve disturbs the layers. Both favour turbulence. Absence of movement cannot raise speed, and a uniform vessel of unchanged area does not add the geometric trigger.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Which feature most clearly marks turbulent flow rather than laminar flow?
options: It appears when the speed is very low
It contains irregular swirls and eddies
It dissipates no energy as the fluid moves
It keeps every layer moving in a straight path
A.explain: Turbulent flow is irregular, with swirls and eddies and mixing between layers. Low speed, no energy loss, and straight layers belong to laminar flow, not turbulence.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Under ordinary resting conditions in a healthy person, blood flow is usually:
options: Vapor flow, with no liquid motion
No flow at all in the arteries
A.explain: At rest in a healthy artery, blood moves in smooth parallel layers, which is laminar flow. It is not vapor, not stationary, and not turbulent in every vessel.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: In steady flow, with no fluid added or removed, what stays the same between two points?
options: The fluid temperature at both points
The vessel diameter at both points
The fluid speed at both points
The flow rate at both points
A.explain: If nothing is added or removed, the flow rate into one section equals the flow rate out of the next. Temperature, diameter, and speed can all change along the path.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: The cross-section of an incompressible vessel falls by a factor of 5. By what factor does the speed rise, in steady flow?
A.explain: For an incompressible fluid, area times speed is constant, so speed rises by the same factor that area falls. A drop by 5 raises speed by 5, not by 2, 10, or 25.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Which body fluids are liquids, and which are gases, in the circulation and the airway?
options: Blood, lymph, and plasma as liquids; oxygen, carbon dioxide, and air as gases
Blood, lymph, and plasma as gases; oxygen, carbon dioxide, and air as liquids
Blood and airway air as liquids; lymph, plasma, and oxygen as gases
Plasma and carbon dioxide as liquids; blood, lymph, and oxygen as gases
A.explain: Blood, lymph, and plasma are liquids. Oxygen, carbon dioxide, and air in the airway are gases. Swapping the two groups, or splitting one group across both states, breaks that pairing.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Blood is treated as which kind of fluid in the continuity relation used for vessels?
options: A gas whose density falls as it speeds up
A solid that keeps a fixed vessel shape
An incompressible liquid of steady density
A fluid whose density doubles in a narrow segment
A.explain: Blood is treated as incompressible, so density stays the same and continuity reduces to area times speed. A gas that thins, a solid, or a density that doubles would not give that reduction.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: In carotid stenosis, why does blood speed rise in the narrowed segment?
options: Hooke's relation stretches the wall, and speed follows the stretch
The continuity relation keeps area times speed constant
Pascal's relation sends the same pressure to every point
Archimedes' relation equals the upward force to displaced weight
A.explain: Speed rises because the narrower area must carry the same flow, so area times speed stays constant. Hooke, Pascal and Archimedes do not set that speed.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Blood flows at 0.20 m/s through a vessel of area 0.030 m². The vessel narrows to 0.010 m². What is the new speed, if the blood is incompressible?
A.explain: Area times speed is constant, so 0.030 × 0.20 = 0.010 × v₂. That gives v₂ = 0.60 m/s.

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: Mass flow rate is written Q = m/Δt, with m the mass. Which unit does that expression give? (Note: mass flow rate ṁ may also be written as Q: Q = ρAv.)
A.explain: Mass divided by time is the kilogram per second. Cubic metre per second is volume flow rate. Kilogram metre per second is momentum, and the newton-second is impulse (not mass flow rate).

A.cat: Chapter 3: Mass Flow Rate and Equation of Continuity
A.q: A vessel narrows from 0.08 m² to 0.02 m². Upstream speed is 0.4 m/s. Downstream speed?
A.explain: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so v₂ = 0.08 × 0.4 / 0.02 = 1.6 m/s. Quartering the area quadruples the speed.

A.q: Which equation correctly states Bernoulli's principle for an ideal fluid along a streamline?
options: P + ½ ρ v² + ρ g h = constant
P + ρ v² + ρ g h = constant
P + ½ ρ v + ρ g h = constant
P × ½ ρ v² + ρ g h = constant
A.explain: Bernoulli's equation for an ideal fluid (steady, incompressible, non-viscous, streamline flow) states that the sum of pressure energy, kinetic energy, and potential energy per unit volume remains constant: P + ½ ρ v² + ρ g h = constant. The term ½ ρ v² is the kinetic energy density. Options that omit the one-half factor, drop the square on velocity, or multiply instead of add do not conserve the total mechanical energy per unit volume.

A.q: Bernoulli's equation applies to an ideal fluid. Answer each condition.
A.explain: An ideal fluid for Bernoulli's equation requires steady flow so the pattern does not change with time, an incompressible fluid so density stays constant, a non-viscous fluid so no energy is lost to internal friction, and streamline paths. Any other condition in each step violates the assumptions and allows energy dissipation or density change.

steps.prompt: Which time condition is required?
Which density condition is required?
Which friction condition is required?
Which path condition is required?

A.q: For an ideal incompressible fluid in a horizontal tube, which statements are true when velocity increases? Select all that apply.
A.explain: In horizontal ideal flow, P + ½ρv² is constant, so rising velocity raises the kinetic energy density and lowers the static pressure. The total mechanical energy density stays constant rather than rising, and the potential energy density does not change because the height of a horizontal tube is fixed.

A.q: In an atherosclerotic stenosis, which sequence of changes occurs in the narrowed arterial segment?
A.explain: Continuity requires that a smaller area produce a higher velocity to keep volume flow rate constant. Bernoulli then requires that the higher velocity produce a lower pressure. Sequences that reverse the velocity or pressure change, or that increase area, contradict the combined continuity and Bernoulli relations observed in stenotic arteries.

A.q: A patient has carotid artery stenosis. Why does blood velocity increase at the stenotic region?
A.explain: The continuity equation states that A₁ v₁ = A₂ v₂ for incompressible flow, so a reduced cross-sectional area forces velocity upward to maintain the same volume flow rate. Bernoulli's principle explains the subsequent pressure drop, not the velocity increase itself. Laplace's law concerns wall tension, and viscosity concerns resistance to shear, neither of which directly sets the local speed from the area change.

A.q: Which device uses Bernoulli's principle to entrain room air and deliver a controlled oxygen concentration?
A.explain: A Venturi mask forces oxygen through a narrow orifice so that the high speed lowers the pressure and draws in a fixed ratio of room air. Nasal cannulas, non-rebreather masks, and simple face masks deliver oxygen by different dilution or reservoir mechanisms and do not rely on the pressure drop from accelerated flow.

A.q: Audible heart murmurs arise when blood flows at high velocity through a narrowed valve because of which process?
options: Turbulent flow generated by the high-speed jet
Laminar flow maintained by the high-speed jet
Reduced viscosity produced by the high-speed jet
Increased wall tension produced by the high-speed jet
A.explain: High velocity through a narrowed valve raises the Reynolds number and produces turbulent eddies whose vibrations are heard as murmurs. Laminar flow is quiet, viscosity is a property of the fluid not generated by speed, and wall tension is governed by Laplace's law rather than the jet itself.

A.q: Doppler ultrasound is a non-invasive technique used primarily to measure which quantities of blood flow?
A.explain: Doppler ultrasound detects the frequency shift of reflected sound waves to determine both the speed and the direction of moving blood. Viscosity, density, wall tension, thickness, temperature, and absolute pressure are not the primary outputs of the Doppler method.

A.q: Water (density 1000 kg/m³) speeds up from 2 m/s to 4 m/s in a horizontal pipe. By how much does the pressure drop?
A.explain: At constant height Bernoulli reduces to P₁ − P₂ = ½ ρ (v₂² − v₁²). Substituting gives ½ × 1000 × (16 − 4) = 6000 Pa. The values 4000 Pa, 8000 Pa, and 2000 Pa result from omitting the one-half factor, doubling the difference of squares, or using only one of the squared velocities.

A.q: Fluid of density 1050 kg/m³ rises 1.5 m at constant speed. What is the approximate pressure drop due to the height change?
A.explain: At constant speed the kinetic terms cancel and P₁ − P₂ = ρ g Δh = 1050 × 9.8 × 1.5 ≈ 15435 Pa. The other figures come from using water density, doubling the height, or halving the product.

A.q: Define viscosity and give its SI unit.

steps.prompt: Viscosity is a fluid's resistance to which type of deformation?
What is the SI unit of viscosity?

A.explain: Viscosity is a fluid's resistance to shear deformation or flow, caused by internal friction between adjacent layers; it relates shear stress to velocity gradient, τ = η(dv/dy). Its SI unit is the pascal-second, Pa·s.

A.q: Which equation correctly relates the force F needed to slide one plate over another through a viscous fluid layer?
A.explain: The viscous force is proportional to area A and velocity v and inversely proportional to the gap y, giving F = η A v / y where η is the coefficient of viscosity. Inverting the velocity-gap ratio or placing area in the denominator reverses the observed dependence.

A.q: Which units are equivalent to the SI unit of dynamic viscosity? Select all that apply.
A.explain: Dynamic viscosity is pressure times time, so Pa·s and its equivalent N·s·m⁻² are correct; in base units it is kg·m⁻¹·s⁻¹. The unit kg·m⁻¹·s⁻² is the pascal itself, and Pa·s⁻¹ divides by time instead of multiplying.

A.q: Shear stress is related to the velocity gradient by which statement?
options: Shear stress equals viscosity times the velocity gradient
Shear stress equals viscosity divided by the velocity gradient
Shear stress equals density times the velocity gradient
Shear stress equals pressure times the velocity gradient
A.explain: Rearrangement of the viscous-force equation yields F/A = η (v/y), so shear stress is the product of viscosity and the velocity gradient. Division, substitution of density, or substitution of pressure would describe different physical quantities.

A.q: An increase in blood viscosity produces which set of circulatory effects?
options: Lower blood flow, greater vascular resistance, and higher cardiac workload
Higher blood flow, lower vascular resistance, and lower cardiac workload
Lower blood flow, lower vascular resistance, and higher cardiac workload
Higher blood flow, greater vascular resistance, and lower cardiac workload
A.explain: Higher viscosity raises the resistance to flow (from Poiseuille's law Q ∝ 1/η), so the same pressure gradient produces less volume flow and the heart must generate a larger pressure difference, increasing its workload. The opposite directions of change reverse the known dependence of flow on viscosity.

A.q: Which changes are expected in polycythemia? Select all that apply.
A.explain: Polycythemia raises red cell concentration, which raises viscosity and therefore vascular resistance. With higher resistance the flow rate for the same pressure difference falls, so it does not rise.

A.q: Compared with normal blood, anemic blood shows which combination of viscosity and oxygen-carrying changes?
options: Reduced viscosity and reduced oxygen-carrying capacity
Increased viscosity and reduced oxygen-carrying capacity
Reduced viscosity and increased oxygen-carrying capacity
Increased viscosity and increased oxygen-carrying capacity
A.explain: Fewer red cells lower both the viscosity (less particle interaction) and the oxygen-carrying capacity (less hemoglobin). The other pairings reverse one or both of these observed effects of anemia.

A.q: Which formula gives the volume flow rate Q of a viscous fluid through a cylindrical tube?
options: Q = π r⁴ ΔP / (8 η L)
Q = π r⁴ ΔP / (4 η L)
Q = π r⁴ ΔP / (2 η L)
Q = π r⁴ η / (8 ΔP L)
A.explain: Poiseuille's law is Q = π r⁴ ΔP / (8 η L). The fourth-power radius dependence, the factor 8, and the placement of viscosity in the denominator are required. Changing the numerical factor to 4 or 2, or inverting the viscosity-pressure placement, each produces an incorrect flow rate.

A.q: If vessel radius doubles while pressure difference, viscosity, and length remain constant, which changes are predicted? Select all that apply.
A.explain: Poiseuille's law gives Q ∝ r⁴, so doubling the radius gives 16 times the flow, the resistance falls to 1/16, and the mean velocity rises by 16/4 = 4 because the area grows 4 times. The line 'Q becomes 8 times larger' uses a cubic dependence instead of the fourth power.

A.q: If the radius of a vessel is halved while all other quantities remain constant, the volume flow rate becomes what fraction of its original value?
A.explain: A factor-of-one-half change in radius multiplies flow by (1/2)⁴ = 1/16. The larger fractions correspond to lower powers of radius and would apply only if the dependence were weaker.

A.q: Which statement correctly summarizes the dependence of volume flow rate on pressure difference, viscosity, and length?
options: Q increases with ΔP and decreases with both η and L
Q decreases with ΔP and increases with both η and L
Q increases with both ΔP and η and decreases with L
Q increases with both ΔP and L and decreases with η
A.explain: From Q = π r⁴ ΔP / (8 η L) the flow rate is directly proportional to the pressure difference and inversely proportional to viscosity and to tube length. Any reversal of these proportionalities contradicts the formula.

A.q: A stenotic carotid artery has a smaller radius. Which effects are expected in the narrowed segment? Select all that apply.
options: Local pressure falls in the stenosis.
Flow rate rises through the segment.
A.explain: Continuity raises velocity when area falls, and Bernoulli lowers local pressure when velocity rises. Poiseuille's law makes resistance rise, not fall, when the radius shrinks, so the flow rate through the segment does not rise.

A.q: For a cylindrical blood vessel, wall tension T is related to internal pressure P and radius r by which equation?
A.explain: Laplace's law for a cylinder states that wall tension equals the product of transmural pressure and radius: T = P r. Division, squaring the radius, or addition each fails to match the force balance on a curved wall.

A.q: Wall stress σ in a thin-walled vessel is given by which expression involving pressure, radius, and wall thickness t?
A.explain: Wall stress is the tension distributed through the wall thickness, so σ = P r / t. Placing thickness in the numerator, multiplying all three quantities, or inverting the entire product reverses the dependence on wall thickness.

A.q: Why must the aortic wall be especially thick and strong?
options: The aorta has a large radius, producing high wall tension
The aorta has a small radius, producing high wall tension
The aorta has a large radius, producing low wall tension
The aorta has a small radius, producing low wall tension
A.explain: Because T = P r, the large radius of the aorta generates high wall tension that must be supported by a thick, strong wall. A small radius would lower tension, and a large radius does not lower tension.

A.q: Which statements correctly apply Laplace's law to a thin-walled cylindrical blood vessel? Select all that apply.
options: Higher P raises T if r is fixed.
A.explain: For a thin-walled cylinder, wall tension is T = Pr, so a higher pressure raises the tension when the radius is fixed, and the wall stress is σ = Pr/t. The line 'T = P / r' inverts the radius dependence; tension grows with radius.

A.q: Reynolds number is defined as the ratio of which two forces?
A.explain: Re = ρ v D / η compares the magnitude of inertial forces to viscous forces. The reciprocal ratio, a pressure-to-gravity comparison, or a surface-tension comparison each describes a different dimensionless group.

A.q: Which formula correctly calculates the Reynolds number for flow in a tube of diameter D?
A.explain: The standard definition is Re = ρ v D / η. Inverting density and viscosity, omitting diameter from the numerator, or rearranging the remaining symbols each fails to recover the correct ratio of inertial to viscous forces.

A.q: A vessel flow has Reynolds number below 2000. Which statements are generally true? Select all that apply.
A.explain: Below Re = 2000 viscous forces dominate and damp disturbances, so the flow is laminar, smooth and layered. Dominant inertial forces and eddies throughout the flow describe high-Re turbulent flow.

A.q: Which changes increase the Reynolds number of blood flow? Select all that apply.
A.explain: Re = ρvD/η, so a rise in velocity raises the Reynolds number. Viscosity is in the denominator, so a rise in viscosity lowers Re, and a fall in diameter or density also lowers it.

A.q: Surface tension is defined as which quantity?
options: The force acting per unit length along the liquid surface
The force acting per unit area on the liquid surface
The energy stored per unit volume in the liquid surface
The pressure difference per unit radius across the surface
A.explain: Surface tension T equals force divided by the length of the line on which the force acts (T = F/L), with units N/m. Force per area is pressure or stress, energy per volume is an energy density, and pressure difference per radius is related to the Laplace pressure jump rather than the definition of T itself.

A.q: Which pair of changes both increase the surface tension of a liquid?
options: Stronger intermolecular forces and lower temperature
Weaker intermolecular forces and higher temperature
Addition of surfactant and higher temperature
Stronger intermolecular forces and addition of surfactant
A.explain: Stronger cohesive forces and lower temperature both raise surface tension. Weaker forces, higher temperature, or the presence of surfactants each lower surface tension.

A.q: Pulmonary surfactant contributes to alveolar stability by which mechanisms? Select all that apply.
A.explain: Surfactant lowers T, and because P = 2T/r for a spherical alveolus, a lower T lowers the pressure needed to keep alveoli open and helps prevent collapse. It does not act by enlarging the alveoli.

A.q: Respiratory distress syndrome in premature infants is caused by which deficiency?
A.explain: Insufficient surfactant leaves surface tension high, so the pressure required to inflate alveoli (P = 2T/r) becomes excessive and the lungs are stiff. Macrophages, type I cells, and capillary blood are not the missing factor in classic neonatal RDS.

A.q: The pressure difference needed to keep a spherical alveolus open is given by which relation?
A.explain: For a spherical interface the Laplace pressure jump is P = 2T/r. Omitting the factor 2, multiplying instead of dividing by radius, or placing an extra 2 in the denominator each fails to satisfy the force balance on a curved liquid film.

A.q: Match each term in Bernoulli's equation to the energy it represents per unit volume.

rightItems.text: Kinetic energy per unit volume
Pressure energy per unit volume
Gravitational potential energy per unit volume
Viscous dissipation per unit volume

A.explain: P is the pressure energy density, ½ ρ v² is the kinetic energy density, and ρ g h is the gravitational potential energy density. Viscous dissipation is absent from the ideal-fluid form of Bernoulli's equation and therefore matches none of the three terms.

A.q: Match each factor in Poiseuille's law to its effect on volume flow rate when the factor increases.

rightItems.text: Flow rate increases strongly (fourth-power dependence)
Flow rate increases in direct proportion
Flow rate decreases in inverse proportion
Flow rate decreases in inverse proportion
Flow rate remains unchanged

A.explain: Radius enters to the fourth power, so flow rises steeply; pressure difference enters to the first power, so flow rises in direct proportion; both viscosity and length appear in the denominator, so flow falls inversely with each. The unmatched line stating that flow remains unchanged fits none of the four factors.

A.q: Match each physical principle to the clinical example that illustrates it.

rightItems.text: Venturi mask delivering controlled oxygen
Polycythemia raising vascular resistance
Small change in arterial radius producing large change in flow
Aneurysm risk from elevated wall tension
Heart murmur from turbulent flow
Neonatal respiratory distress from surfactant deficiency
Doppler measurement of absolute pressure

A.explain: Bernoulli's principle underlies the Venturi mask, elevated viscosity underlies the resistance of polycythemia, the r⁴ dependence of Poiseuille's law underlies large flow changes from small radius changes, Laplace's law underlies aneurysm wall tension, Reynolds number distinguishes the turbulent flow of murmurs, and surface tension (lowered by surfactant) underlies alveolar stability and its failure in RDS. Doppler ultrasound measures velocity, not absolute pressure, so that line remains unmatched.

A.q: A carotid artery narrows because of atherosclerosis. Follow the physical consequences step by step.

steps.prompt: What happens to blood velocity in the narrowed segment?
Given the velocity change just identified, what happens to local pressure?
What happens to vascular resistance through the narrowed segment?

A.explain: Continuity requires that the reduced area raise velocity so that A v remains constant. Bernoulli's relation then requires that the higher velocity lower the local pressure. Poiseuille's law requires that the reduced radius raise resistance (Q ∝ r⁴), so less flow reaches the distal tissue. Options that reverse any of these three changes contradict the respective equations.

A.q: Match each Bernoulli term to its energy type.

rightItems.text: ½ρv²
ρgh
P
Heat per volume

A.explain: Motion gives ½ρv², position gives ρgh, and compression gives P. Heat is not part of the Bernoulli sum.

A.q: Consider an alveolus whose lining fluid contains pulmonary surfactant. Answer each step.

steps.prompt: How does the presence of surfactant change the surface tension of the lining fluid?
Given that change in surface tension, what happens to the pressure required to keep the alveolus open?
What is the clinical consequence for alveolar stability?

A.explain: Surfactant lowers surface tension T. Because the pressure needed to inflate a spherical alveolus is P = 2T/r, a lower T reduces the required pressure. The reduced collapsing tendency keeps the alveoli open. Options that raise tension, raise required pressure, or produce collapse reverse the known action of surfactant.

A.q: A tube of radius 1 mm carries fluid at a certain flow rate. If the radius is increased to 2 mm with no other change, the new flow rate is how many times the original rate?
A.explain: Flow rate scales with the fourth power of radius, so doubling the radius multiplies flow by 16. The smaller multipliers correspond to lower powers and are incorrect.

A.q: Two vessels have the same internal pressure. Vessel A has twice the radius of vessel B. How does the wall tension of A compare with that of B?
options: Wall tension of A is twice that of B
Wall tension of A is half that of B
Wall tension of A equals that of B
Wall tension of A is four times that of B
A.explain: From T = P r, tension is directly proportional to radius when pressure is fixed, so doubling the radius doubles the tension. Halving, equality, or a four-fold change would require a different functional dependence.

A.q: In F/A = η v/y, the quantity F/A is which type of stress?
A.explain: The force F acts along the surface of the fluid layer, parallel to the plate, so F/A is a shear stress. Its unit is Pa, like pressure, but tensile, compressive and bulk stresses act at right angles to a surface or on a whole volume.

A.q: Which expression defines the coefficient of viscosity η?
A.explain: Viscosity is shear stress divided by velocity gradient: η = (F/A) / (v/y) = Fy/(Av). This rearranges F = ηAv/y and gives the unit Pa·s. Multiplying the two ratios, inverting them, or swapping A and y does not match F = ηAv/y.

A.q: Which formula gives the force to move a plate over a fluid layer?
A.explain: Force is viscosity times area times velocity over separation: F = ηAv/y. It rises with area and speed and falls with gap.

A.q: Which expression gives the mean velocity of viscous flow through a tube?
options: v̄ = π ΔP r² / (8 η L)
A.explain: The mean velocity is v̄ = ΔP r² / (8ηL). Multiplying it by the area πr² gives Q = πr⁴ΔP/(8ηL), so the π and the r⁴ belong to the flow rate, not to the velocity. A factor of 4 instead of 8 does not match Poiseuille's result.

A.q: Poiseuille's law can be built from flow rate, tube area and mean velocity. Answer each step.
A.explain: Volume flow rate is area times mean velocity, Q = A v̄. A round tube has A = πr². With v̄ = ΔP r²/(8ηL), Q = πr² × ΔP r²/(8ηL) = πr⁴ΔP/(8ηL), so the two r² factors combine to r⁴. That is why flow depends so strongly on radius.

steps.prompt: Which relation links volume flow rate to area and mean velocity?
Given Q = A v̄, what is A for a round tube of radius r?
Multiplying πr² by ΔP r²/(8ηL) leaves the radius raised to which power?

A.q: Re = ρ v D / η. Identify each Greek symbol in this formula.
A.explain: ρ is the Greek letter rho and stands for fluid density; it is easily misread as the Latin p. η is the Greek letter eta and stands for viscosity; it looks like the Latin n. The numerator ρvD reflects inertial force and the denominator η reflects viscous force, so Re is their ratio.

steps.prompt: What is the name of the Greek letter ρ?
Which property does rho represent in this formula?
What is the name of the Greek letter η?
Which property does eta represent in this formula?

A.q: In the wall stress relation σ = P r / μ, what does μ represent?
A.explain: μ is the wall thickness. Wall tension T = P × r is spread through the thickness of the wall, giving wall stress σ = Pr/μ. Thickness is also commonly written t, as in σ = Pr/t. A thicker wall therefore carries less stress for the same pressure and radius.

A.q: Which follow from Laplace's law for vessels? Select all that apply.
options: A large aortic radius raises wall tension.
Higher pressure raises arterial wall stress.
A thicker wall lowers wall stress.
A smaller aneurysm raises rupture risk.
A.explain: Tension tracks pressure and radius, so a big aorta and high pressure raise wall load, while a thicker wall lowers stress. Aneurysm risk rises with larger, not smaller, radius.

A.q: Which is the SI unit of surface tension?
A.explain: Surface tension is force per unit length, γ = F/L, so its SI unit is N/m. N/m² is the pascal, used for pressure and stress, N·m is the unit of work or torque, and Pa·s is the unit of viscosity.

A.q: Surface tension in N/m is equivalent to which unit of energy per area?
A.explain: 1 N/m = 1 N·m/m² = 1 J/m², so surface tension can also be read as surface energy per unit area. J/m³ is energy per volume, W/m² is intensity, and J/m equals the newton.

A.q: A liquid has a surface tension of 72 dyne/cm. What is this in N/m?
A.explain: 1 dyne/cm = 10⁻³ N/m, because 1 dyne = 10⁻⁵ N and 1 cm = 10⁻² m. So 72 dyne/cm = 72 × 10⁻³ N/m = 0.072 N/m, close to the value for water at room temperature.

A.q: Surface tension is commonly written with which Greek letter?
A.explain: Surface tension is commonly written γ, gamma, and is also written T, as in T = F/L. η is used for viscosity, ρ for density, and μ here for wall thickness in the wall stress relation.

A.q: Water rises in a narrow glass tube. Which comparison of forces explains this?
options: Cohesion within water exceeds adhesion to glass
Adhesion to glass exceeds cohesion within water
Viscous drag exceeds adhesion to glass
Gravity on water exceeds cohesion within it
A.explain: Adhesive force is attraction between molecules of different substances, here water and glass. Cohesive force is attraction between molecules of the same substance. Because adhesion to glass is stronger than cohesion within water, water wets the glass, curves up at the edges and rises. Mercury shows the opposite and falls.

A.q: In capillary rise h = 2γ cos θ / (ρ g r), what does θ represent?
A.explain: θ is the contact angle between the liquid surface and the tube wall. It shows how well the liquid wets the solid, that is, adhesion compared with cohesion. A small θ means good wetting and a large rise. Measuring h, r and θ lets the surface tension γ be found.

A.q: Match each force or quantity to its description.

rightItems.text: Attraction between molecules of one substance
Shows how well a liquid wets a solid
Attraction between molecules of two different substances
2γ cos θ / (ρ g r)
Force per unit area on a surface

A.explain: Cohesion holds molecules of the same liquid together; adhesion attracts molecules of different substances, such as a liquid and its container wall. The contact angle shows the balance between them, that is, how well the liquid wets the solid. Capillary rise is h = 2γ cos θ / (ρ g r). Force per unit area is pressure or stress, not one of these.

A.q: Match each surface tension concept to its medical importance.

rightItems.text: Prevents collapse of air sacs
Blood collection and microfluidic devices
Liquid surface tends to contract
Explains lung mechanics
Breathing difficulty in premature infants
Measures blood flow velocity

A.explain: Surface tension, T = F/L, is the tendency of a liquid surface to contract. Pulmonary surfactant lowers surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse. Respiratory distress syndrome is surfactant deficiency causing breathing difficulty in premature infants. Capillary action, surface tension plus adhesion, is used in blood collection and microfluidic devices. P = 2T/r for alveolar stability explains lung mechanics. Measuring blood flow velocity is Doppler ultrasound.

A.q: Which of the following correctly lists the three fundamental types of waves?
A.explain: Waves are classified into three fundamental types: mechanical waves, which require a material medium; electromagnetic waves, which can travel through a vacuum; and matter waves, which are associated with particles. Longitudinal and transverse are directional descriptions of mechanical waves, not fundamental types. Sound, light, and water are examples of waves rather than a classification scheme. Thermal and electrical are not wave categories.

A.q: Sound waves are best described as:
A.explain: Sound is a mechanical wave because it requires a material medium, and it is longitudinal because the particles of the medium vibrate in the same direction as the wave propagates. Transverse waves have particle motion perpendicular to propagation. Electromagnetic waves do not require a medium, and matter waves are associated with particles, not sound.

A.q: Which statement about sound propagation is correct?
options: Sound crosses a vacuum at a slightly reduced speed
Sound cannot cross a vacuum, since it needs a medium
Sound crosses a vacuum only at the lowest frequencies
Sound crosses any vacuum freely and needs no medium
A.explain: Sound is a mechanical wave, so it propagates by displacing the particles of a medium such as air, water, or steel. A vacuum contains no particles to displace, so sound cannot travel through it at any speed or any frequency. The speed of sound depends on the medium and is not a fixed value that applies everywhere.

A.q: In a sound wave traveling through air, the particles of the medium vibrate in which direction relative to the wave's propagation?
options: Perpendicular to the direction of wave travel
At 45 degrees to the direction of wave travel
In the same direction as the wave travels
In a circle around the direction of travel
A.explain: A longitudinal wave is defined by particle displacement that is parallel to the direction of energy propagation. As the sound wave moves forward, it creates regions of compression and rarefaction by pushing and pulling air molecules along the same axis. Perpendicular vibration describes a transverse wave, such as a wave on a string or light.

A.q: The pitch of a sound is determined by its:
A.explain: The frequency of a sound wave is the number of cycles that pass a point per second, and this is what the human ear perceives as pitch. A higher frequency corresponds to a higher pitch, such as a police siren, while a lower frequency corresponds to a lower pitch. Amplitude determines loudness, not pitch. Speed and wavelength are related to frequency through the wave equation but are not the perceptual quantity.

A.q: The loudness of a sound is most directly related to its:
A.explain: Amplitude is the height of the wave above the rest position and represents the maximum displacement of particles from equilibrium. A larger amplitude carries more energy and is perceived as louder. Frequency determines pitch, wavelength is the spatial length of one cycle, and time period is the inverse of frequency.

A.q: The time required to complete one full vibration or cycle is called the:
A.explain: The time period is defined as the time taken for one complete cycle of vibration. It is the reciprocal of frequency, as given by the relation Time period = 1 / frequency. Frequency is the number of cycles per second, wavelength is the spatial length of one cycle, and amplitude is the maximum displacement from the rest position.

A.q: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz. What is its time period?
A.explain: Time period is the inverse of frequency, so T = 1 / f = 1 / 50 Hz = 0.02 s. This means one complete cycle takes 0.02 seconds. The line 50 s confuses period with frequency, 0.5 s uses an incorrect division, and 2 s is the inverse of 0.5 Hz rather than 50 Hz.

A.q: Which equation correctly relates wave velocity (v), frequency (f), and wavelength (λ)?
A.explain: Wave velocity is the speed at which a disturbance moves through a medium. It equals the product of frequency, which is how many cycles pass per second, and wavelength, which is the distance of one cycle. This gives the fundamental wave equation v = f × λ. The other options represent incorrect rearrangements such as dividing frequency by wavelength or adding the two quantities.

A.q: A tuning fork vibrates with a frequency of 512 Hz. If the speed of sound in air is 343 m/s, what is the wavelength of the sound waves?
A.explain: Using the wave equation v = f × λ, the wavelength is λ = v / f. Substituting the values gives λ = 343 m/s / 512 Hz ≈ 0.67 m. The line 1.49 m divides frequency by velocity instead of velocity by frequency, 175,616 m multiplies the two values, and 0.33 m uses a velocity that is roughly half the correct value.

A.q: A sound wave has a wavelength of 0.5 m and travels at a speed of 340 m/s. What is its frequency?
A.explain: Rearranging the wave equation v = f × λ gives f = v / λ. Substituting the values gives f = 340 m/s / 0.5 m = 680 Hz. The line 170 Hz divides by 2 instead of 0.5, 340 Hz ignores the wavelength, and 0.0015 Hz inverts the division.

A.q: The speed of a sound wave in a medium with bulk modulus B and density ρ is given by:
A.explain: The speed of sound in a medium is determined by how stiff and how dense the medium is. The bulk modulus B measures stiffness, or resistance to compression, and density ρ measures inertia. The relationship is v = √(B / ρ). A high bulk modulus increases the speed, while a high density decreases it. The other options either omit the square root or invert the ratio.

A.q: In which of the following media does sound travel the fastest?
options: A perfect vacuum with no particles
A.explain: The speed of sound is generally greatest in solids, less in liquids, and least in gases. This is because the particles in a solid are packed more closely together, allowing them to transmit the vibrational energy more quickly. Steel is a solid, so sound travels faster in it than in water or air. Sound cannot travel in a vacuum at all.

A.q: The speed of sound in air at 0°C is 331 m/s. What is its approximate speed at 20°C?
A.explain: The speed of sound in air increases with temperature. At 0°C it is 331 m/s, and at 20°C it rises to approximately 343 m/s. The line 331 m/s repeats the value at 0°C, 1482 m/s is the speed of sound in water at 20°C, and 965 m/s is the speed of sound in helium.

A.q: The speed of sound in water is 1402 m/s at 0°C and 1482 m/s at 20°C. This shows that:
options: The speed of sound decreases with increasing temperature
The speed of sound increases with increasing temperature
The speed of sound is independent of temperature
A.explain: The two values show that as the temperature of water rises from 0°C to 20°C, the speed of sound increases from 1402 m/s to 1482 m/s. This temperature dependence is general: warmer media generally transmit sound faster because the particles have more thermal energy and can pass the disturbance along more quickly. Water clearly transmits sound at 0°C, so the fourth option is false.

A.q: The speed of sound in helium is 965 m/s and in hydrogen is 1284 m/s. These values are:
options: Lower than the speed of sound in air at the same temperature
Higher than the speed of sound in air at the same temperature
Equal to the speed of sound in air at the same temperature
Lower than the speed of sound in water at the same temperature
A.explain: The speed of sound in air at 20°C is 343 m/s. Helium at 965 m/s and hydrogen at 1284 m/s are both much higher. This is because these gases have very low density, and since speed is proportional to the square root of bulk modulus divided by density, a lower density raises the speed. The values 965 m/s and 1284 m/s are also lower than the speed of sound in water, which is 1482 m/s, but the comparison asked here is against air.

A.q: The speed of sound in seawater at 20°C and 3.5% salinity is:
A.explain: The speed of sound in seawater at 20°C and 3.5% salinity is 1522 m/s. This is slightly higher than the speed in fresh water at the same temperature, which is 1482 m/s, because dissolved salts increase the bulk modulus of the water. The value 1402 m/s is for fresh water at 0°C, and 5941 m/s is the speed of sound in steel.

A.q: The speed of sound in steel is approximately:
A.explain: Steel is a solid with a high bulk modulus and moderate density, giving a speed of sound of approximately 5941 m/s. The value 343 m/s is for air at 20°C. The values 6000 m/s and 6420 m/s are the speeds of sound in granite and aluminum, two other solids. The high speed in steel reflects the strong intermolecular forces that allow rapid transmission of vibrational energy.

A.q: What is the audible frequency range for a typical human being?
A.explain: The human ear is sensitive to sound waves with frequencies ranging from approximately 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. One line narrows both bounds, using 22 Hz as the lower limit and 18,000 Hz as the upper limit. Another line widens both bounds, using 18 Hz and 22,000 Hz. A further line keeps the correct lower bound of 20 Hz but sets the upper bound too low at 18,000 Hz. Frequencies above 20,000 Hz are called ultrasonic, and those below 20 Hz are infrasonic.

A.q: Sound waves with frequencies greater than 20,000 Hz are classified as:
A.explain: Ultrasound is defined as sound with a frequency above the upper limit of human hearing, which is 20,000 Hz. Infrasonic waves are below 20 Hz, and the audible range is between these two limits. Subsonic refers to speeds slower than the speed of sound, not to frequency.

A.q: Sound waves with frequencies below 20 Hz are classified as:
A.explain: Infrasonic waves are those with frequencies below the lower limit of human hearing, which is 20 Hz. Ultrasonic waves are above 20,000 Hz, and the audible range lies between these two limits. Supersonic refers to speeds greater than the speed of sound, not to frequency.

A.q: Which statement correctly compares ultrasound imaging with X-ray and CT imaging?
options: Ultrasound and X-ray are non-ionizing, but CT is ionizing
Ultrasound is ionizing, but X-ray and CT are non-ionizing
Ultrasound and CT are ionizing, but X-ray is non-ionizing
Ultrasound is non-ionizing, unlike X-ray and CT
A.explain: Ultrasound imaging uses high-frequency sound waves, which are mechanical vibrations and therefore non-ionizing. X-ray and CT imaging use ionizing electromagnetic radiation, which can damage biological molecules. This distinction is clinically important because it makes ultrasound safer for repeated use, such as in obstetric imaging. One line wrongly classifies X-ray as non-ionizing, the second reverses the classification of ultrasound and X-ray, and the third wrongly classifies CT as ionizing while calling X-ray non-ionizing.

A.q: A physician needs to image deep abdominal structures and obstetric patients. Which ultrasound frequency range is most appropriate?
A.explain: Lower ultrasound frequencies penetrate deeper into tissue but provide lower resolution. For deep abdomen and obstetric imaging, 2.5 MHz is recommended. Higher frequencies such as 7.5 MHz, 10.0 MHz, and 15.0 MHz provide better resolution but do not penetrate as deeply, so they are used for superficial structures such as breast, thyroid, and musculoskeletal imaging.

A.q: Which ultrasound frequency is recommended for imaging superficial structures such as the thyroid and superficial veins?
A.explain: For superficial structures such as the breast, thyroid, superficial veins, and superficial masses, a higher frequency of 10.0 MHz is recommended. Higher frequencies provide better spatial resolution but do not penetrate deeply. The lower frequencies 2.5 MHz, 3.5 MHz, and 5.0 MHz are used for deeper structures such as the abdomen, obstetrics, and vascular imaging.

A.q: A tuning fork labeled 136.1 Hz is used clinically for which purpose?
options: To measure the speed of sound in body tissue
To test hearing and vibration sensitivity
To determine the density of body fluids
A.explain: A tuning fork of 136.1 Hz is used to assess a patient's hearing and vibration sensitivity, which can indicate nerve damage. The low frequency produces a vibration that can be felt as well as heard. It is not used to measure the speed of sound in tissue, calibrate ultrasound machines, or determine fluid density.

A.q: For a wave traveling at a constant speed, how are frequency and wavelength related?
options: They are independent of each other
A.explain: The wave equation v = f × λ states that the product of frequency and wavelength is constant for a given wave speed. Therefore, if the speed is constant, frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional: as one increases, the other must decrease by the same factor. This is expressed as f ∝ 1 / λ.

A.q: The Doppler effect describes the change in the observed frequency of a wave when:
options: The source and observer move relative to each other
The wave travels through a vacuum with no medium present
The amplitude of the wave increases over time alone
The wave reflects off a stationary surface nearby
A.explain: The Doppler effect is the change in frequency or wavelength of a wave for an observer moving relative to its source. If the source and observer approach each other, the observed frequency increases; if they move apart, the observed frequency decreases. The effect is not related to a vacuum, amplitude, or reflection from a stationary object.

A.q: An ambulance is approaching you at a constant speed with its siren on. What change in the sound do you perceive?
options: The frequency increases, and the pitch rises
The frequency decreases, and the pitch drops
The frequency remains constant, but the loudness drops
The frequency first drops, then rises
A.explain: As the source moves toward the observer, the sound waves are compressed, leading to a higher observed frequency and a higher pitch. As the source moves away, the waves are stretched, leading to a lower observed frequency and a lower pitch. The loudness may decrease with distance, but the defining perceptual change is the shift in pitch.

A.q: If either the detector or the source is moving, the emitted frequency f and detected frequency f' are related by which equation?
A.explain: The general Doppler formula accounts for motion of both the detector and the source: f' = f × ((v ± v_D) / (v ± v_S)), where v is the speed of sound, v_D is the speed of the detector, and v_S is the speed of the source. The signs are chosen according to whether each is moving toward or away from the other. The other options either fix one of the speeds at zero or use incorrect sign combinations.

A.q: A source of sound moves with speed v_S toward a stationary observer. If v is the speed of sound in air, which formula gives the observed frequency f'?
A.explain: When the source moves toward a stationary observer, the observed frequency is higher than the emitted frequency. The formula uses a minus sign in the denominator to represent the source catching up to the waves it emits, compressing them. The formula is f' = f × (v / (v - v_S)). A plus sign in the denominator would describe a receding source, and the other forms are incorrect arrangements.

A.q: A source of sound moves with speed v_S away from a stationary observer. If v is the speed of sound in air, which formula gives the observed frequency f'?
A.explain: When the source moves away from a stationary observer, the observed frequency is lower than the emitted frequency. The formula uses a plus sign in the denominator to represent the waves being stretched out behind the receding source. The formula is f' = f × (v / (v + v_S)). A minus sign in the denominator would describe an approaching source, and the other forms are incorrect arrangements.

A.q: A stationary source emits sound at frequency f. An observer moves toward the source with speed v_D. If v is the speed of sound, which formula gives the observed frequency?
A.explain: When the observer moves toward a stationary source, the observer encounters more wavefronts per second, so the observed frequency is higher. The formula places the detector speed in the numerator with a plus sign: f' = f × ((v + v_D) / v). If the observer moved away, the numerator would use a minus sign. The other options incorrectly place the detector speed in the denominator or use the wrong sign.

A.q: Shock waves are produced when a source of sound moves:
options: At exactly the speed of sound in the medium
At a speed less than the speed of sound
At a speed greater than the speed of sound
At a speed equal to the speed of light
A.explain: Shock waves are generated when a source travels at a speed greater than the speed of sound in the medium, meaning v_S > v. This is supersonic speed. The wavefronts lag behind the source and pile up, forming a cone-shaped shock wave. The resulting sonic boom is heard when this wave reaches an observer. A source moving at exactly the speed of sound does not produce a shock wave, and no object with mass can travel at the speed of light.

A.q: The Mach number is defined as the ratio of:
options: The speed of sound to the speed of the source
The speed of the source to the speed of sound
The frequency of the source to the speed of sound
The amplitude of the wave to the speed of sound
A.explain: The Mach number (M_a) is a dimensionless quantity that compares the speed of an object moving through a fluid to the local speed of sound. It is defined as M_a = v_S / v, where v_S is the speed of the source and v is the speed of sound. An aircraft flying at Mach 2 is traveling at twice the speed of sound.

A.q: An aircraft flies at Mach 2.3 through air in which sound travels at 340 m/s. What is the speed of the aircraft?
A.explain: The Mach number is the source speed divided by the speed of sound, so the source speed is M × v = 2.3 × 340 m/s = 782 m/s. 148 m/s divides instead of multiplying, 342 m/s adds 2.3 to 340, and 680 m/s is Mach 2.

A.q: A sonic boom is heard when:
options: A source crosses the sound barrier at Mach one
A shock wave from a supersonic source arrives
A source travels at a low subsonic speed
A source emits sound continuously while at rest
A.explain: A sonic boom is the sound heard when a shock wave, produced by a supersonic source, reaches an observer. The shock wave is the cone-shaped pileup of wavefronts trailing the source. It is not produced by a source moving at exactly the speed of sound, at subsonic speeds, or while at rest.

A.q: The visible condensation cloud around a supersonic aircraft is caused by:
options: A local pressure rise produced by the passing shock wave
A local pressure drop produced by the passing shock wave
A local temperature rise produced by friction with the air
A local temperature drop produced by the aircraft exhaust
A.explain: The shock wave causes a sudden decrease in air pressure and temperature. This local cooling causes water molecules in the air to condense, forming a visible fog or cloud. A pressure rise or a temperature rise would warm the air rather than cool it, so neither would produce condensation. A temperature drop from the exhaust is not the mechanism, because the exhaust itself is hot.

A.q: Which Mach number range corresponds to supersonic waves?
A.explain: Supersonic conditions occur when the speed of the source exceeds the speed of sound, which corresponds to M_a > 1. M_a = 0 describes a stationary source, and M_a < 1 describes subsonic speeds. M_a = 1 is the sonic speed, at which the source travels exactly at the speed of sound.

A.q: The Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics establishes the concept of:
A.explain: The Zeroth Law states that if two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third body, then they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This law provides the basis for defining temperature and justifies the use of a thermometer. If body A and body B are both in equilibrium with a thermometer T, they have the same temperature and will not exchange heat when brought into contact.

A.q: Two bodies are in thermal equilibrium when:
options: They have the same mass and volume
They are at the same temperature
They have the same volume and shape
They are both in the solid state
A.explain: Thermal equilibrium means the two bodies are at the same temperature throughout, so no net heat flows from one to the other. Mass, volume, and state of matter are not conditions for thermal equilibrium. This definition is the foundation of temperature measurement.

A.q: Which temperature represents absolute zero?
A.explain: Absolute zero is the lowest possible temperature, where thermal motion of particles reaches its minimum. It is defined as 0 Kelvin (0 K). On the Celsius scale, this is -273.15 °C, and on the Fahrenheit scale, it is -459.67 °F. The other options are not absolute zero.

A.q: The triple point of water is the unique temperature and pressure at which:
options: Water boils and freezes at the same time
Ice, water, and vapor coexist in equilibrium
Ice and vapor coexist while liquid is absent
Liquid and vapor coexist while ice is absent
A.explain: The triple point of a substance is a specific combination of pressure and temperature where its solid, liquid, and gas phases can coexist in thermal equilibrium. For water, this occurs at a temperature of 0.01°C and a pressure of 0.6 kPa. This is a key reference point for thermodynamic temperature scales.

A.q: On the phase diagram of water, the critical point occurs at approximately:
A.explain: The critical point on the phase diagram of water is the end point of the liquid-vapor boundary, occurring at approximately 374°C and 22,089 kPa. Beyond this point, the liquid and gas phases become indistinguishable. The values 0.01°C and 0.6 kPa describe the triple point, 100°C and 101 kPa describe normal boiling, and 0°C and 0.6 kPa are not a specific labeled point on the diagram.

A.q: A patient has a body temperature of 39°C. What is this temperature in degrees Fahrenheit?
A.explain: To convert from Celsius to Fahrenheit, the formula is T_F = (9/5) × T_C + 32. Substituting 39°C gives T_F = (9/5) × 39 + 32 = 70.2 + 32 = 102.2°F. The line 99.0°F uses 37°C, 107.6°F uses an incorrect multiplier, and 93.2°F uses an incorrect conversion.

A.q: Convert a temperature of 15°C to the Kelvin scale.
A.explain: The conversion from Celsius to Kelvin is T_K = T_C + 273. Substituting 15°C gives T_K = 15 + 273 = 288 K. The line 258 K subtracts 15 from 273 instead of adding, 273 K ignores the Celsius value, and 300 K uses an incorrect offset.

A.q: Convert a temperature of 300 K to the Celsius scale.
A.explain: The conversion from Kelvin to Celsius is T_C = T_K - 273. Substituting 300 K gives T_C = 300 - 273 = 27°C. The line 573°C adds 273 instead of subtracting, 27 K incorrectly labels the result as Kelvin, and 300°C ignores the offset entirely.

A.q: At what temperature do the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales have the same numerical value?
A.explain: The Celsius and Fahrenheit scales coincide at -40°, where T_C = T_F = -40. This can be verified by setting T_C = T_F in the conversion formula T_F = (9/5) × T_C + 32 and solving for the temperature, which gives -40. The other options are reference points on one scale or the other but not points of coincidence.

A.q: Normal body temperature is 37.0°C. What is this in degrees Fahrenheit?
A.explain: Using the conversion T_F = (9/5) × T_C + 32, substituting 37.0°C gives T_F = (9/5) × 37.0 + 32 = 66.6 + 32 = 98.6°F. The line 100.4°F corresponds to 38°C, 95.0°F corresponds to 35°C, and 104.0°F corresponds to 40°C.

A.q: The temperature near 0 K is significant because:
options: Thermal motion reaches its minimum value
All gases become liquids at this point
The Celsius and Fahrenheit scales coincide
A.explain: Near absolute zero, which is 0 K or -273.15°C, the thermal motion of particles reaches its minimum possible value. This is the lowest temperature theoretically attainable. Water freezes at 273.15 K, not at 0 K. Not all gases become liquids at this temperature, and the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales coincide at -40°, not at absolute zero.

A.q: Match each characteristic of a sound wave to its correct description.

rightItems.text: The number of cycles that occur per unit of time.
The maximum displacement of a particle from its rest position.
The time required to complete a single cycle of vibration.
The distance between two successive points that are in the same phase.
The speed at which the disturbance propagates.

A.explain: Wavelength is the spatial length of one complete cycle, such as the distance between two adjacent crests. Amplitude is the height of the wave, representing the maximum displacement from equilibrium, which relates to loudness. Frequency is the number of complete cycles per second, measured in hertz, which relates to pitch. The time period is the time for one full cycle and is the inverse of frequency. The remaining option describes wave velocity.

A.q: Match each temperature scale to its correct defining property or reference point.

rightItems.text: Water boils at 100 degrees and freezes at 0 degrees.
Water boils at 212 degrees and freezes at 32 degrees.
Absolute zero is the starting point, and there are no negative values.
The scale is defined by the triple point of water.

A.explain: The Kelvin scale is an absolute temperature scale where 0 K is absolute zero, the theoretical point of minimum thermal energy, and it has no negative values. The Celsius scale is defined by the freezing point of water at 0°C and its boiling point at 100°C at standard atmospheric pressure. The Fahrenheit scale uses different reference points, with water freezing at 32°F and boiling at 212°F. The triple point of water is a specific thermodynamic reference, not the general defining property of these scales in everyday use.

A.q: Match each wave formula to the quantity it defines or the relationship it expresses.

rightItems.text: The speed of sound in a medium from its bulk modulus and density.
The relationship between wave velocity, frequency, and wavelength.
The ratio of the speed of a source to the speed of sound.
The time required for one complete vibration from the frequency.
The change in observed frequency from source and detector motion.

A.explain: The equation v = f × λ relates wave velocity to frequency and wavelength. The equation T = 1 / f gives the time period from the frequency. The equation v = √(B / ρ) gives the speed of sound in a medium from its bulk modulus and density. The Mach number M_a = v_S / v is the ratio of the source speed to the speed of sound. The remaining option describes the Doppler effect, which is expressed by a different formula.

A.q: Each ultrasound frequency is named. Choose its imaging class.

steps.prompt: 2.5 MHz is used for which class of imaging?
10.0 MHz is used for which class of imaging?
options: Thyroid, superficial veins, and musculoskeletal imaging
Deep abdomen, obstetric, and gynecological imaging
General abdomen, pelvic, and vascular imaging

A.explain: Lower frequencies penetrate deeper, so 2.5 MHz is the choice for deep abdomen and obstetric work. Higher frequencies give finer detail, so 10.0 MHz is the choice for thyroid, superficial veins, and musculoskeletal imaging. The remaining lines name the opposite depth class.

A.q: A sound source moves relative to a stationary observer. Choose the correct formula at each step.

steps.prompt: The source moves toward the stationary observer. Which formula gives the observed frequency?
The source now moves away from the stationary observer. Which formula gives the observed frequency?

A.explain: When the source approaches a stationary observer the waves are compressed, so the denominator uses a minus sign: f' = f × (v / (v - v_S)). When the source recedes the waves are stretched, so the denominator uses a plus sign: f' = f × (v / (v + v_S)). Placing the source speed in the numerator or reversing the sign each fails to match the direction of motion.

A.q: Each Mach-number range is named. Choose the wave class it belongs to.

steps.prompt: M_a < 1 belongs to which class?
M_a ≈ 1 belongs to which class?
M_a > 1 belongs to which class?

A.explain: M_a < 1 means the source is slower than sound and is subsonic (M_a = 0 would be a source at rest). M_a ≈ 1 is the sonic boundary and is called transonic. M_a > 1 means the source is faster than sound and is supersonic. The remaining lines name the other speed classes.

A.q: Each temperature scale is named. Choose its defining property.

steps.prompt: The Kelvin scale is defined by which property?
options: Absolute zero as the starting point with no negative values
Water freezes at 0 degrees and boils at 100 degrees
Water freezes at 32 degrees and boils at 212 degrees
The triple point of water as the sole fixed point

steps.prompt: The Celsius scale is defined by which property?
options: Water freezes at 0 degrees and boils at 100 degrees
Water freezes at 32 degrees and boils at 212 degrees
The critical point of water as the upper limit
The triple point of water as the sole fixed point

A.explain: Kelvin begins at absolute zero and has no negative values. Celsius is fixed by the freezing and boiling points of water at 0 °C and 100 °C. The remaining lines name the fixed points of the other scales.

A.q: The frequency of a sound wave is set by the:
A.explain: The vibrating source sets the emitted sound frequency. Observer motion causes Doppler shift, while medium warmth and detector sensitivity affect propagation or reception, not the emitted frequency.

A.q: Sound waves travel much slower than which waves?
options: Mechanical waves, which require a medium
Infrasonic waves, which have low frequency
A.explain: Sound travels much slower than light, which is an electromagnetic wave. Mechanical waves include sound, matter waves are particle-associated, and infrasonic waves are low-frequency sound.

A.q: One hertz equals which vibration rate?
A.explain: Hertz is the SI unit of frequency: 1 Hz equals one vibration or cycle per second. The other rates use the wrong time unit, invert period, or give speed.

A.q: Wave velocity is also called which speed?
A.explain: Wave velocity is the speed of the travelling disturbance, also called propagation speed. Particle, source, and detector speeds describe objects, not the disturbance.

A.q: Ultrasound imaging is described as which type of technique?
A.explain: Ultrasound is non-invasive, non-ionizing, and fast to acquire. Invasive, ionizing, and slow descriptions contradict those stated features.

A.q: Ultrasound image acquisition is described as:
A.explain: Acquisition is easy and fast, using non-ionizing sound. Slow, invasive, ionizing, delayed, random, and unsafe descriptions contradict the stated acquisition.

A.q: Ultrasound imaging visualizes which features of organs and vessels?
A.explain: Ultrasound shows structure, movement, and function. Pressure replaces structure, temperature replaces movement, and density replaces function; those quantities belong to shock-wave changes.

A.q: Match each ultrasound frequency to its main imaging use.

rightItems.text: General abdomen, obstetric, and gynecological imaging
Vascular, breast, and pelvic imaging
Breast and thyroid imaging
Superficial structures and musculoskeletal imaging

A.explain: 3.5 MHz is for general abdomen, obstetric, and gynecological imaging; 5.0 MHz for vascular, breast, and pelvic imaging; 7.5 MHz for breast and thyroid imaging; 15.0 MHz for superficial structures and musculoskeletal imaging.

A.q: Clinical ultrasound imaging commonly uses which frequency range?
A.explain: Clinical ultrasound uses 2 MHz to 15 MHz. The 20 Hz to 20 kHz range is audible sound, 20 kHz to 2 MHz is below clinical imaging, and the reversed range is false.

A.q: A scanner uses 3.8 MHz in tissue where sound speed is 1.5 km/s. Find wavelength.
A.explain: Wavelength equals speed divided by frequency. Using 1500 m/s and 3.8 × 10⁶ Hz gives 3.95 × 10⁻⁴ m, or 0.39 mm. Other choices shift the decimal point.

A.q: Besides sound, which wave type is included in the Doppler description?
A.explain: The Doppler description names sound and also light waves. Matter, shock, and infrasonic waves are wave categories in the chapter but not the named Doppler example.

A.q: Colour Doppler echocardiography is used to show which of these?
A.explain: Colour Doppler echocardiography shows blood flow in vessels and the heart. Kidney stones relate to shock waves, tissue tumors to ultrasound scanning, and water vapor to phase changes.

A.q: A supersonic source leaves wave fronts in a cone with the source at the:
A.explain: The cone-shaped shock region has the moving source at its vertex. The base, centre, and edge describe other parts of the cone, not the source position.

A.q: Shock waves produce a sudden change in which quantities?
A.explain: Shock waves abruptly change pressure, temperature, and density. Frequency replaces pressure, wavelength replaces temperature, and period replaces density; those are ordinary wave-cycle quantities.

A.q: Which statement about shock waves is correct?
A.explain: Shock waves are high-amplitude pressure waves faster than sound and can break kidney stones. Slower travel, low amplitude, and Mach 0 occurrence contradict shock-wave facts.

A.q: The triple point of water occurs at which temperature?
A.explain: The triple point is 273.16 K, where ice, liquid water, and vapor coexist. 273.15 K is the usual freezing approximation, while 0 K and -273.15 °C describe absolute zero.

A.q: Water triple-point pressure on the phase diagram is which value?
A.explain: The triple-point pressure is 0.006 atm, which equals 611.73 Pa. The other choices keep the numbers but attach the wrong unit or decimal scale.

A.q: A body temperature of 35 °C converts to which Fahrenheit value?
A.explain: Using TF = 9/5 TC + 32 gives 63 + 32 = 95 °F. The other values omit the offset, add wrongly, or repeat the Celsius number.

A.q: Which of the following correctly states the laws of reflection?
options: The incident ray, the normal, and the reflected ray lie in one plane, and the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
The incident ray, the normal, and the reflected ray lie in separate planes, and the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
The incident ray, the normal, and the reflected ray lie in one plane, and the angle of incidence is twice the angle of reflection
The incident ray and the reflected ray lie on the same side of the normal, and the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
A.explain: Reflection follows three rules: the incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence, and the reflected ray all lie in one plane; the incident and reflected rays are on opposite sides of the normal; and the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. The line 'The incident ray, the normal, and the reflected ray lie in separate planes, and the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection' breaks the coplanar rule. The line 'The incident ray, the normal, and the reflected ray lie in one plane, and the angle of incidence is twice the angle of reflection' states an incorrect angle relationship. The line 'The incident ray and the reflected ray lie on the same side of the normal, and the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection' places both rays on the same side of the normal.

A.q: A light ray strikes a plane mirror at 35 degrees to the mirror surface. What is the angle of reflection, measured from the normal?
A.explain: Angles of incidence and reflection are measured from the normal. A ray at 35 degrees to the surface is at 90 − 35 = 55 degrees to the normal, so the angle of incidence is 55 degrees and, by the law of reflection, so is the angle of reflection. 35 degrees is the angle from the surface, 70 degrees doubles it, and 145 degrees is 180 − 35.

A.q: An image that cannot be projected onto a screen because light does not actually pass through it is called:
A.explain: A virtual image is formed by the apparent divergence of light rays. The rays do not actually converge at the image location, so the image cannot be captured on a screen. A real image is formed where light rays actually converge and can be projected. Inverted and magnified describe image orientation and size, not whether light physically passes through the image point.

A.q: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a plane mirror. Where is the image formed, and what are its properties?
options: 20 cm behind the mirror, virtual and the same size as the object
20 cm in front of the mirror, real and the same size as the object
40 cm behind the mirror, virtual and magnified compared with the object
10 cm behind the mirror, virtual and diminished compared with the object
A.explain: For a plane mirror, the image distance equals the object distance, so the image appears 20 cm behind the mirror. The image is virtual because light does not actually pass through it, and it is the same size as the object. The line '20 cm in front of the mirror, real and the same size as the object' incorrectly places the image in front and calls it real. The lines '40 cm behind the mirror, virtual and magnified compared with the object' and '10 cm behind the mirror, virtual and diminished compared with the object' give incorrect distances and sizes.

A.q: A spherical mirror whose reflecting surface curves inward, toward the centre of the sphere, is called:
A.explain: A concave mirror has its reflecting surface on the inside of the spherical curve, facing the centre of curvature. A convex mirror reflects from the outside of the curve, away from the centre. A plane mirror is flat, and a cylindrical mirror has a different geometry not covered by the spherical mirror definitions.

A.q: A spherical mirror whose reflecting surface curves outward, away from the centre of the sphere, is called:
A.explain: A convex mirror has its reflecting surface on the outside of the spherical curve, facing away from the centre of curvature. A concave mirror reflects from the inside of the curve. A plane mirror is flat, and a parabolic mirror has a different non-spherical geometry.

A.q: For a concave mirror, a parallel beam of light incident on the mirror converges after reflection at a single point called the:
A.explain: When a parallel beam of light strikes a concave mirror, the reflected rays converge at the focal point, denoted by F. The centre of curvature is the centre of the sphere from which the mirror is cut. The principal axis is the line through the centre of curvature and the vertex. The vertex is the central point on the mirror surface itself.

A.q: The distance between the central point of a spherical mirror and its focus is called the:
A.explain: The focal length, denoted by f, is the distance from the mirror's central point to the focal point. The radius of curvature is the distance from the mirror surface to the centre of curvature and equals twice the focal length. Object distance and image distance measure the positions of the object and image relative to the mirror.

A.q: The relationship between the focal length f and the radius of curvature r of a spherical mirror is:
A.explain: Using the geometry of a spherical mirror, the focal point lies halfway between the mirror surface and the centre of curvature, so f = r / 2. The line 'f = 2r / 1' doubles the radius. The line 'f = r / 4' quarters it. The line 'f = 4r / 1' multiplies the radius by four.

A.q: A concave mirror has a focal length of 25 cm. What is its radius of curvature?
A.explain: Rearranging f = r / 2 gives r = 2f. Substituting f = 25 cm gives r = 2 × 25 = 50 cm. The line '12.5 cm' halves the focal length instead of doubling it, '25 cm' repeats the focal length, and '100 cm' quadruples it.

A.q: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 40 cm. What is its focal length?
A.explain: Using f = r / 2, substituting r = 40 cm gives f = 40 / 2 = 20 cm. The line '80 cm' doubles the radius instead of halving it, '40 cm' repeats the radius, and '10 cm' quarters it.

A.q: For a concave mirror, when an object is placed outside the focal point, the image formed is:
options: Virtual, upright, and larger than the object at all times
Real, inverted, and variable in size with object distance
Virtual, inverted, and smaller than the object at all times
Real, upright, and smaller than the object at all times
A.explain: When the object is beyond the focal point of a concave mirror, the reflected rays actually converge, forming a real image. That image is inverted. Its size depends on where the object sits: beyond twice the focal length it is smaller, at twice the focal length it is the same size, and between twice the focal length and the focal point it is larger. The line 'Virtual, upright, and larger than the object at all times' describes the case when the object is inside the focal point. The lines 'Virtual, inverted, and smaller than the object at all times' and 'Real, upright, and smaller than the object at all times' mix properties that do not occur together for this mirror.

A.q: For a concave mirror, when an object is placed inside the focal point, the image formed is:
A.explain: When the object lies between the focal point and the mirror surface, the reflected rays diverge and must be extended backward to meet. The resulting image is virtual, upright, and larger than the object. The line 'Real, inverted, and diminished' describes a real image from an object outside the focal point. The lines 'Real, upright, and magnified' and 'Virtual, inverted, and diminished' mix real with upright or virtual with inverted, combinations that do not occur for this mirror.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the image formed by a convex mirror?
